newsitem.title: Mexico: Mexican volcano may force villagers' evacuation.
newsitem.headline: Mexican volcano may force villagers' evacuation.
newsitem.dateline: ON THE SLOPES OF POPOCATEPETL, Mexico 1997-07-01

text.p: Thousands of frightened villagers kept a wary eye on this rumbling giant volcano on Tuesday, awaiting possible evacuation after its biggest eruption in 72 years.
Hundreds of soldiers fanned out across slopes shrouded in cloud and ash after Monday night's explosion to check on the mountain's condition and assess the danger of mudslides.

"Our soldiers are climbing the volcano to check the situation. Since there is so much cloud and ash we need a firsthand look at its condition," said Gen. Garrido Abreu, directing operations at the 17,890-foot (5,452-metre) volcano.

About 150 soldiers dressed in heavy clothes against biting cold struggled up the steep, ash-covered slopes while military helicopters circled nearby, unable to view the crater because of the swirling clouds.

Farther down, some villagers dressed in bright woollen ponchos packed their possessions to be ready for evacuation. Others, doubting the danger, refused to budge. Many were listening to local radio reports telling them to stay inside and await word from the authorities on whether or not to abandon their homes in the shadow of the cone-shaped mountain.

Three-quarters of Mexico City's airport runways were closed on Tuesday as trucks bulldozed away piles of ash from Popocatepetl's most violent explosion since 1925. The snow-capped mountain belched red-hot rocks and blew clouds of smoke into the sky late on Monday, covering the capital 33 miles (55 km) away in a layer of ash. Winds blew the fine gray grit as far east as the Caribbean port of Veracruz.

"All of a sudden the ground started shaking and we heard a series of violent explosions," said Irene Rosales, a 52-year-old peasant woman who was picking mushrooms with her husband two-thirds of the way up the volcano when it blew.

"We began running down the hill but then stones as big as my hand came raining down on top of us and the cloud of ash surrounded us," she said. "We could hardly breathe. It smelled of sulphur and sewage. ... I never thought I'd see my home again."

In Rosales' village of San Pedro Nexapa, residents were gathered by the local church for an annual festival in honour of their patron saint. They were celebrating with a band and a small bullfight when the volcano erupted, sending them scrambling for cover.

"People began to panic and everyone ran to their homes," said Evarista Martinez, 65. The village is divided by a centuries-old swathe of solid volcanic rock that serves as a stark reminder of its precarious position.
Julian Perez, an 83-year-old corn farmer on his way to check his field at the volcano's base, said he had never seen Popocatepetl so angry.
"I know it well. About 70 years ago it used to smoke and smoke, but it never spat out rocks like this," he said, adding that even his donkey no longer wanted to climb its slopes.

In nearby Amecameca, a town of 40,000 that looked semideserted on Tuesday, most shops remained closed while the remaining residents swept ash and volcanic rock off streets, wearing masks to protect themselves against the dirty air.

There were small signs on nearby roads indicating the evacuation route but many residents complained that the government had not given them any instructions. Even if they knew which way to run, it seemed unlikely many would go, believing their fate to be determined by God and the volcano.

"One sacrifices so much just to get a roof over one's head. How can we leave that behind? What will become of our chickens and pigs?" Martinez said, clutching a black shawl and glancing anxiously toward the volcano.
